topics.title: What is Hashing?
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for What is Hashing?.

pages.title: Hashing
pages.content:
## What is hashing?

Hashing maps a key to a compact lookup location through a hash function. Hash tables use that location to make average-case insertion and lookup very fast.

The important idea is not that hashing guarantees `O(1)` in every case; it is that a well-designed hash table normally provides **average-case `O(1)`** lookup, insertion, and deletion.

Common uses include frequency counting, membership tests, grouping, caches, indexes, and duplicate detection.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

checkpoint.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of a hash table?
options: It maps keys to buckets so average-case lookup and insertion can be very fast.
It guarantees worst-case O(1) time for every lookup regardless of collisions.
It stores every possible key in a dense array before any lookup can occur.
It removes the need for a collision-resolution strategy.
checkpoint.explanation: Hash tables use a hash function to map keys to buckets. Good implementations provide average-case constant-time operations, while collisions still need to be handled.

pages.title: How Does Hashing Work
pages.content:
## How hashing works

A hash table combines three ideas:

1. A **key**, such as an integer or string.
2. A **hash function**, which maps the key to a bucket/index.
3. A **table** that stores the associated entry.

For a teaching hash function such as `h(x) = x % 10`, the value `38` maps to bucket `8`. Different keys can map to the same bucket, so a hash table also needs a collision strategy.

A production hash table should also keep the load factor under control so lookups remain efficient.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: Using Hashing to Optimize counting frequency
pages.content:
## Frequency counting with hashing

Instead of comparing every pair of elements to count frequencies, maintain a hash table from value to count.

For each value `x`, perform `freq[x]++`.

This changes the usual quadratic pair-counting approach into an average-case `O(N)` pass, with `O(K)` extra memory for `K` distinct values.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: Frequency using Hashing
pages.content:
## Frequency using hashing

A hash map is useful when values can be large or sparse. You do not need an array indexed by the entire value range.

For example, values near `10^9` can still be counted with an `unordered_map<int,int>` because the table stores only values that actually occur.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: Use Hashing
pages.content:
## Prefix hashing for beautiful pairs

Suppose a pair `(i, j)` is beautiful when `i < j` and `A[i] = A[j]^2`.

As we scan from left to right, the hash table stores the frequency of values already seen. For the current `A[j]`, we only need the count of `A[j] * A[j]` in that prefix.

This turns repeated searches into one average-case constant-time hash lookup per element.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: MCQ
pages.content:
## What makes a good hash function?

A good hash function should be deterministic and should distribute typical keys across buckets as evenly as practical.

Collisions cannot be completely eliminated when the key space is larger than the table's bucket space. The goal is to avoid pathological clustering and keep operations efficient.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: Conclusion
pages.content:
## Hashing trades memory for speed

A direct frequency array is excellent when the possible values lie in a small, dense range. It becomes wasteful when values may be as large as `10^9`.

A hash map stores only the keys that actually appear. This is the standard way to handle large or sparse value ranges while retaining average-case constant-time lookup.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

topics.title: Hash collision and Hashmaps
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Hash collision and Hashmaps.

pages.title: Collision
pages.content:
## Hash collisions

A collision occurs when different keys map to the same bucket. With `h(x) = x % 10`, both `38` and `88` map to bucket `8`.

Collisions are a normal part of hash-table operation. They are not an error by themselves; the data structure must resolve them correctly.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

checkpoint.question: What is a collision in hashing?
options: Two different keys produce the same table bucket.
A hash table runs out of CPU registers.
A key is inserted twice into a sorted vector.
A lookup is performed without a hash function.
checkpoint.explanation: A collision occurs when distinct keys map to the same bucket, so the table needs a collision-resolution method.

pages.title: Resolving Collisions
pages.content:
## Collision resolution: separate chaining

With separate chaining, each bucket stores a collection of entries that hashed to that bucket.

If two keys collide, both remain accessible through the same bucket. The lookup first computes the bucket and then searches that bucket's chain.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: More Collision Resolution Techniques
pages.content:
## Open addressing

Open addressing stores entries directly inside the table. On collision, a probing sequence searches for another available slot.

**Linear probing** checks consecutive positions. **Quadratic probing** uses increasing offsets. The probing rule must be deterministic, and deletion requires special care so searches do not terminate too early.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use the hashing technique taught on this page to make lookup, counting, or collision handling efficient and predictable.

pages.title: Built-In Hashing Data Structures
pages.content:
## Built-in hashing data structures

Most languages provide built-in hash-based structures:

- C++: `unordered_map`, `unordered_set`
- Java: `HashMap`, `HashSet`
- Python: `dict`, `set`

They hide the bucket and collision-management details behind a convenient API. Choose a map when you need key-to-value associations and a set when you only need membership.

questions.question: What does a hash function produce for a key?
options: A bucket/index used to locate the key in a table.
A sorted copy of the entire table.
A guaranteed unique number for every possible key.
A recursive traversal of all stored keys.
questions.explanation: A bucket/index used to locate the key in a table.

questions.question: Which statement about hash-table complexity is accurate?
options: Lookup is always O(log N).
Average-case lookup can be O(1), but collisions can affect performance.
Lookup is always O(N log N).
Hashing guarantees O(1) in the worst case.
questions.explanation: Average-case lookup can be O(1), but collisions can affect performance.

questions.question: Why use a hash map for frequency counting?
options: It stores a compact mapping from each observed value to its count.
It sorts all values before counting them.
It removes the need to read the input.
It requires an array for every possible integer.
questions.explanation: It stores a compact mapping from each observed value to its count.

questions.question: What is a collision?
options: Two different keys map to the same bucket.
The same key is read twice.
A table contains an empty bucket.
A lookup uses a string key.
questions.explanation: Two different keys map to the same bucket.

questions.question: Why can direct indexing be wasteful for values near 10^9?
options: The index array could be enormous even when only a few values occur.
Large values cannot be stored in C++.
Hash tables cannot store integers.
Frequency counting needs recursion.
questions.explanation: The index array could be enormous even when only a few values occur.

questions.question: What does h(x)=x mod M do?
options: It maps x into one of the M bucket indices 0 through M-1.
It sorts x.
It encrypts x.
It guarantees no collisions.
questions.explanation: It maps x into one of the M bucket indices 0 through M-1.

questions.question: What property helps a hash function distribute keys well?
options: It should spread typical keys across buckets instead of clustering them.
It should map every key to bucket 0.
It should preserve alphabetical order.
It should use recursion for every key.
questions.explanation: It should spread typical keys across buckets instead of clustering them.

questions.question: What does a frequency map entry `freq[x]` represent?
options: The number of buckets in the table.
The number of times x has been observed.
The hash value of x.
The position of x in sorted order.
questions.explanation: The number of times x has been observed.

questions.question: When scanning for A[i] = A[j]^2, what should be stored before processing j?
options: All future values.
Only the largest value.
Frequencies of values from indices smaller than j.
Sorted pairs of indices.
questions.explanation: Frequencies of values from indices smaller than j.

questions.question: Why must multiplication for x*x use a wide integer type in many problems?
options: Hashing requires floating point.
The square can exceed the range of a 32-bit integer.
Maps only accept 64-bit keys.
Modulo cannot be applied to int values.
questions.explanation: The square can exceed the range of a 32-bit integer.

questions.question: Which structure is appropriate when only membership is needed?
options: A hash set such as C++ `unordered_set`.
A matrix of all possible values.
A stack only.
A sorted linked list only.
questions.explanation: A hash set such as C++ `unordered_set`.

questions.question: What does separate chaining store at one bucket?
options: A collection of entries sharing that bucket.
Only the smallest key.
Only one entry with all others discarded.
A second hash table that is always sorted.
questions.explanation: A collection of entries sharing that bucket.

questions.question: What is linear probing?
options: Checking subsequent table positions until an available slot is found.
Recursively hashing the key until it changes.
Sorting all keys before insertion.
Storing every collision in a tree.
questions.explanation: Checking subsequent table positions until an available slot is found.

questions.question: What is the main risk of linear probing?
options: Primary clustering can build long runs of occupied slots.
It cannot store integers.
It always requires recursion.
It cannot detect duplicate keys.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of a hash map for large sparse values?
options: Only observed keys need storage.
It allocates all possible values.
It guarantees sorted iteration.
It eliminates collisions.
questions.explanation: Only observed keys need storage.

questions.question: What is a collision-resolution method?
options: A rule for storing multiple keys that map to one bucket.
A method for sorting a graph.
A rule for deleting all duplicates.
A method for compressing strings.
questions.explanation: A rule for storing multiple keys that map to one bucket.

questions.question: Why can two unequal keys have the same modulo hash?
options: The bucket range is smaller than the possible key space.
Modulo always returns the original key.
Only strings collide.
Because the keys are necessarily equal.
questions.explanation: The bucket range is smaller than the possible key space.

questions.question: What operation does `unordered_map::count(k)` help answer in this course?
options: Whether key k is present in the map.
Whether every bucket is empty.
Whether all keys are sorted.
Whether a key is prime.
questions.explanation: Whether key k is present in the map.

questions.question: What is the purpose of rehashing?
options: To change the bucket layout to keep the table efficient as it grows.
To reverse every key.
To convert a map into a stack.
To remove all collisions permanently.
questions.explanation: To change the bucket layout to keep the table efficient as it grows.

questions.question: Which statement about collisions is correct?
options: Collisions are expected; the table must resolve them correctly.
A collision means the input is invalid.
Collisions never occur with integers.
Collisions make hashing unusable.
questions.explanation: Collisions are expected; the table must resolve them correctly.
